text:
A: Hiya! Oh, can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, I can hear you. Hello. Sorry, I wasn't sure if I had to press something.
A: No, you're fine, I think it just starts. I'm Rachel, I'm in Lancaster.
B: I'm Denise. St Helens.
A: Oh, not far then! Practically neighbours. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was rubbish at it, honestly. I got about halfway and then just sort of sat there staring at the shapes.
B: I didn't do very well either, I don't think. I kept second-guessing myself. I'm not sure what it was meant to be testing really.
A: Me neither. I'm choosing to believe it was testing something I'm not good at on purpose. Erm, so what do you do, Denise? If you don't mind me asking.
B: No, that's alright. I'm a dental technician. So I make the crowns and bridges and dentures for the dentists, in a little lab in town. I've been there, oh, over twenty-five years now.
A: Twenty-five years! That's amazing. So you actually make the teeth? Like with your hands?
B: Yeah, sort of. They send us the impressions and we do a model and build it up from that. It's very fiddly. You've got to get the fit right or it's no good to anybody. I like it, though. I've got my bench and my radio on, and I just get on with it.
A: That sounds so calming, actually. My job's the opposite, it's all noise. I work at an arts centre, so I run workshops, family days, bits of touring theatre. Last week I had a hall full of retired blokes doing drama games, and one of them did this brilliant impression of a seagull, and that was it, nobody could get back on track. Sorry, I'm going on.
B: No, no, it sounds lovely. I'd be terrified doing that, standing up in front of people.
A: You'd be surprised, you know? Most people are terrified at first, that's sort of the whole point. Are you not one for singing or anything?
B: Well, I sing in the church choir at Christmas and Easter. But that's different, you're all together, nobody's looking at you.
A: Oh, I'm in a choir! Community one, we rehearse in a church hall. I'm an alto.
B: Are you? I'm alto too, I suppose. I can't get up to the high bits.
A: Nobody can, that's why we're altos. I actually said when I saw your picture, you reminded me of the ladies in my choir. In a good way, I mean.
B: Oh, that's nice. I thought you looked like someone from church, funnily enough.
A: Ha! That's brilliant. Was that a jigsaw on your table? I was squinting at it.
B: It was, yeah. It's a thousand-piece one of a harbour. All boats. I'm stuck on the sky, it's all the same blue.
A: Oh no, the sky's always the worst bit. I've got a quilt that's been nearly done for two years, so I can't really talk about finishing things.
B: Two years? You'll get there.
A: Joe, my partner, says it'll be done for our retirement. What are you having for your tea tonight? Sorry, random question, I'm just starving.
B: I made a big pan of scouse on Sunday, so it'll be that again, I should think. I have it most of the week.
A: Oh, that sounds perfect for this weather. We'll probably have a chippy tea, it's Friday, isn't it? No, sorry, it's Thursday. See, this is me.
B: I do like a chippy tea. And a barm with chips, if I'm being naughty.
A: A chip barm is the best thing ever invented, I'll fight anyone on that.
B: My mum says they're no good for you, but she still has half of mine.
A: Do you live near your mum, then?
B: About ten minutes. I go round most days. She's eighty-one now, so I sort of keep an eye.
A: Aw, that's lovely of you. My mum's in Preston, I don't get down as much as I should, to be honest. I always mean to, and then
B: It's hard when you're busy, isn't it. I don't know really, I just
